newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore meets China Premier, witness business deals.
newsitem.headline: Gore meets China Premier, witness business deals.

text.p: China Premier Li Peng urged the United States on Tuesday to play a more positive world role and Vice President Al Gore set the seal on a warming in battered ties by presiding over a multi-million dollar aircraft sale.
Gore witnessed a lucrative boom in U.S. sales and investment in China that overshadowed a simmering scandal over alleged Chinese funding of U.S. Democratic Party politicians.
"We had a very productive and energetic talk," Gore told reporters after his first meeting with Premier Li Peng in the cavernous Great Hall of the People.

"There are a number of issues that I would like to discuss... all of them are issues that can best be discussed here among ourselves," said Gore, the most senior U.S. official to visit China since Beijing crushed student-led protests in Tiananmen Square in 1989.

Gore did not say whether he raised the thorny issues of human rights and alleged Chinese donations to the Democratic presidential re-election campaign last year, but stressed the importance of maintaining a peace process.
"The non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction is a critical goal of the United States," Gore said.
China's Li sounded a note of caution, reflecting China's concern about superpower politics and spreading U.S. influence.
"China has high respect for the United States," Li said.

"We believe the United States, the biggest developed country in the world, should play a more positive role in international affairs," Li said. "The importance of our relations serves the interests of both peoples."

In a sign of the rapidly improving ties between the world's top superpower and its fastest-growing Pacific neighbour, the two leaders witnessed the signing of two multi-million dollar contracts for U.S. business in China.
Boeing Co signed a deal to sell five 777-200 jets worth $685 million to China's international carrier, Air China.

Analysts said the Chinese decision to buy the new-generation airliners now was almost certainly based not only on aviation needs but on a thaw in ties since Sino-U.S. relations chilled in 1995 and early 1996 amid disputes over human rights and Taiwan.
In the Boeing deal, three of the 777-200s are to be delivered to Air China by the end of 1998 and the other two in 1999.
Gore also witnessed the signing of a formal pact in which General Motors Corp launches a long-delayed joint venture with Shanghai Automotive Industry Corp to build medium-sized cars.
The $1.3 billion motor project in Shanghai will be shared equally by the two corporations. The pact won initial go-ahead in 1995 but final approval was subject to lengthy delays.

Officials dismissed reports that Gore hesitated to attend the ceremony because of allegations that China had tried to influence last year's U.S. presidential election by illegally funnelling cash to support President Bill Clinton's campaign.
"These agreements... are proof positive that there is greater economic cooperation between the United States and China," said Ginny Terzano, Gore's press secretary.
Gore's meetings with Beijing leaders were aimed at strengthening a recent Sino-U.S. rapprochement, but his talks appeared likely to be darkened by the funding scandal.

The Washington Post has reported that the Federal Bureau of Investigation warned six members of Congress last year that they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign contributions from foreign corporations.
Under a third agreement signed on Tuesday, China will formally allow Washington to maintain a consulate in Hong Kong after 150 years of British rule ends at midnight on June 30.
